title: Parents in Alpine School District raise concerns about 'hazardous' school walking routes

Some parents in the Alpine School District are raising concerns about school walking routes they say are hazardous and longer than the threshold used to determine whether their children qualify for bus service.
Some parents in the Alpine School District are raising concerns about school walking routes they say are hazardous and longer than the threshold used to determine whether their children qualify for bus service. Kimberly Contreras lives just inside the two-mile cutoff for her son to qualify for a bus to Lake Mountain Middle School.
Utah schools race to finish summer preparations before students returnContreras said much of the route runs along Redwood Road and includes busy intersections, construction and long stretches with little to no shade.
“It angers me because it’s not necessary,” Contreras said. “There is no shade along about 90% of the route that they’re walking. There are no trees. There’s no way for them to cool off at all.
” She said those concerns become more pronounced during the winter, when students may leave for school before sunrise.
“They will walk the first half of their walk while it is still dark outside and below freezing temperatures,” Contreras said. “They have come out, they have walked throughout with us,” she said. “They have agreed on all of the hazardous concerns and conditions that we’ve experienced.
”In one area near Westlake High School, students cannot cross at the intersection closest to their neighborhood because there is no crosswalk, and the opposite side of the road does not have a sidewalk. To cross safely, parents say students instead have to backtrack about half a mile to a crosswalk, cross the road, and then walk another roughly mile and a half toward the school, bringing the total distance to about two miles.
Alpine School District Transportation Director Rex Brimhall said bus eligibility is primarily determined by distance. Elementary students generally qualify if they live more than 1.5 miles from school, while secondary students qualify if they live more than two miles away. Brimhall said the district can consider hazardous conditions when establishing some additional routes for elementary-age students, but funding those routes can be difficult.
“We do take into account some of the hazardous conditions that might be in existence, and if that’s the case, then we establish some bus routes for them,” Brimhall said. “The difficult thing is we don’t really get reimbursed for much of the ineligible people or the hazardous routes. ” For secondary students who do not qualify based on distance, Brimhall said there is no hazardous-route exception.
Brimhall said qualifying bus routes receive some reimbursement from the state, though not necessarily the full cost. If the district decides to provide transportation for students who do not meet the state eligibility criteria, Brimhall said it has to find another way to pay for it.
“We have to pay for the buses, the drivers, the gas, the fuel, etc.,” he said. “So that money has to come from somewhere. ” The district uses state-approved routing software to calculate the distance between a student’s home and school. Brimhall said those calculations do not simply use Google Maps or measure from one front door to another.
“It’s from nearest public access of the home to the nearest public access to the school, and that’s the property access, not the doors,” he said. “It can be very specific and very accurate where one house could qualify and the neighbor next door may not,” he said. That calculation does not necessarily account for the complete distance a student ultimately walks when the designated route requires detours to reach safe crossings.
Asked specifically whether backtracking to a crosswalk is included in the two-mile calculation, Brimhall said no.Contreras said the geography around her neighborhood illustrates the problem. A privately owned, fenced-off hill divides the area and forces students to walk around it to get to school. That same area is also under construction, which, at points, obstructs the sidewalk along Redwood Road where her son has to walk. Pieces of that sidewalk are also unfinished.
“Blanket codes, blanket rules, blanket laws don’t work,” she said. “Our topography here is so different from, say, Salt Lake City. ” She said parents want hazardous conditions and the distance children actually have to walk to carry more weight in determining whether they qualify for transportation.
“We wish we could transport everybody,” he said. “ are the safest way to get kids to and from school, but there has to be some type of criteria established to identify who does and who doesn’t qualify. ” He also said the district is operating with tighter transportation resources than it has in the past, citing a bus driver shortage and budgetary constraints.
“There was a time when we just had an abundance of drivers, and it didn’t hurt to cover those ineligible routes,” Brimhall said. “Now, it just has to become tighter and more efficient. ” For parents who want the eligibility criteria or distance calculations changed, Brimhall said the Utah State Board of Education is the appropriate place to raise those concerns.
“I would love to employ many more bus drivers and pay them to do that. We just don’t have that ability,” he said. For students who are walking long distances to school, Brimhall recommends starting a “walking school bus,” where you walk with the same group daily, or carpooling.
